pr_body:
Fixes #21543. This produces a file than can then be verified with signify:

```
$ signify-openbsd -V -p pubkey -x sigfile -m archive
```
pr_comments:
Tested the `minisig` command a bit -- it seems to output signature files with the suffix `.minisig`. So maybe we should stick to that, and not use `.sig`, to make our lives easier. 

How does the `signify-openbsd` behave ?

> Tested the `minisig` command a bit -- it seems to output signature files with the suffix `.minisig`. So maybe we should stick to that, and not use `.sig`, to make our lives easier.
> 
> How does the `signify-openbsd` behave ?

`signify-openbsd` uses `.sig` as described in its manpage https://man.openbsd.org/signify.1

From what I see `signify` is the older format as it got introduced in 5.5 which came out ages ago. This being said, `minisign` seems older than its github history. I'm at a loss for a clear sign of which format should have precedence.
closing in order to re-trigger travis

issue_context.title: feature: use minisign to sign binaries
issue_context.body:
From Thomas Ptacek (https://latacora.singles/2019/07/16/the-pgp-problem.html ) : 

> Signing Packages
>
> Use Signify/Minisign. Ted Unangst will tell you all about it. It’s what OpenBSD uses to sign packages. It’s extremely simple and uses modern signing. Minisign, from Frank Denis, the libsodium guy, brings the same design to Windows and macOS; it has bindings for Go, Rust, Python, Javascript, and .NET; it’s even compatible with Signify.


About minisign: https://jedisct1.github.io/minisign/

Minisign is compatible with `signify` used by OpenBSD

The todo's would be: 

- [ ] Make some dummy key and make available to builders
- [ ] Make the builders generate the signature file, based off the dummy key
- [ ] Swap to a real key, publish pub sig on download page
